# QML done right {#sec-qml}

QML looks like a layout language, but it is a language for relationships: this item is half
as wide as that one, this button is enabled while that list is not empty. Writing good QML
means stating relationships and keeping everything else in C++.

## Bindings, not assignments {#sec-bindings}

A property written with a colon is a **binding**. It stays true: whenever the right side
changes, QML re-evaluates it.

```qml
Rectangle {
    id: panel
    width: parent.width / 2          // a binding: follows the parent, forever

    MouseArea {
        anchors.fill: parent
        onClicked: panel.width = 300   // an assignment: replaces the binding
    }
}
```

After the click, `panel` has a fixed width of 300, and resizing the window no longer resizes
it. Most layout bugs in QML come from an assignment where a binding was meant. If a value
should follow something, bind it. If the user changes it, change the *source* of the
binding, usually a property in C++, instead of overwriting the binding.

::: {.callout-important}
## Never assign to a bound property
An assignment from JavaScript removes the binding without any warning. To change a bound
value, change its source. If a property really needs both, restore the binding with
`Qt.binding()`, or better, move that state into C++.
:::

::: {.more}
**Read more:** [Property binding](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/qtqml-syntax-propertybinding.html)
:::

## Components with a clear interface {#sec-components}

A reusable component works like a function: data goes in through properties, intent comes
out through signals. It never reaches into its parent or into ids defined elsewhere.

```{.qml filename="Swatch.qml"}
AbstractButton {
    id: swatch

    required property color ink   // input: whoever uses Swatch must set it
    signal picked(color ink)       // output: reports what happened

    implicitWidth: 28
    implicitHeight: 28
    onClicked: swatch.picked(swatch.ink)

    background: Rectangle {
        radius: width / 2
        color: swatch.ink
    }
}
```

The component only reports that it was picked; its user decides what that means:

```qml
Swatch {
    ink: "#e5484d"
    onPicked: ink => page.penColor = ink
}
```

A component written this way works anywhere, and a test can create it on its own.

::: {.more}
**Template:** the `Swatch` inline component in `src/canvas/CanvasPage.qml`

**Read more:** [QML component design](https://www.kdab.com/qml-component-design/)
:::

## Typed QML that tools can check {#sec-typed-qml}

QML can be as loose as JavaScript or as strict as C++. Write it strict, and qmllint and the
QML compiler can check every name and type at build time; the compiler can then turn your
bindings into C++.

```{.qml filename="SketchbookPage.qml"}
pragma ComponentBehavior: Bound                     // bound to this file

Page {
    id: root

    required property SketchbookViewModel viewModel   // typed and required

    function rename(row: int, name: string): void {   // typed signature
        root.viewModel.rename(row, name)              // qualified lookup
    }
}
```

Each line replaces a guess with a fact the tools can check: no name that "should exist"
somewhere above, no untyped argument, no lookup that depends on where the component is used.

Make qmllint fail on any warning and run it in CI, so a typo fails like a C++ typo does.

::: {.more}
**Template:** `.qmllint.ini`

**Read more:** [qmllint](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/qtquick-tool-qmllint.html)
:::

## Lists come from models {#sec-lists}

A `ListView` creates delegates only for the rows that are visible, and drops them as they
scroll out of view (`reuseItems: true` recycles them instead). Its data comes from a
**model**, and each delegate receives the data of its row as required properties:

```qml
ListView {
    id: list
    model: root.viewModel.model

    delegate: ItemDelegate {
        required property int index
        required property string name   // one property per model role
        required property int strokeCount

        width: list.width
        text: name
        onClicked: root.viewModel.open(index)
    }
}
```

Expose collections as models (@sec-item-models), never as a property holding a whole list:
a model can report "row 3 changed", a list property can only say "everything changed".

::: {.more}
**Template:** `src/sketchbook/SketchbookPage.qml`

**Read more:** [Models and views in Qt Quick](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/qtquick-modelviewsdata-modelview.html)
:::

## Positioning: anchors, layouts, positioners {#sec-positioning}

Qt Quick offers three ways to place items. Pick one per container.

| Tool | Use it for |
|---|---|
| **Anchors** (`anchors.fill`, `anchors.centerIn`) | relating an item to its parent or a sibling |
| **Layouts** (`RowLayout`, `ColumnLayout`, `GridLayout`) | sharing space among items that resize |
| **Positioners** (`Row`, `Column`, `Grid`) | stacking items of fixed size |

```qml
RowLayout {
    anchors.fill: parent          // anchors place the layout
    Label {
        text: qsTr("Sketchbook")
        Layout.fillWidth: true    // takes the free space
    }
    ToolButton { icon.source: "info.svg" }
}
```

::: {.more}
**Read more:** [Positioning in Qt Quick](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/qtquick-positioning-topic.html)
:::

## Keep JavaScript small {#sec-javascript}

JavaScript in QML is glue. A handler calls one method; an expression formats one value.

```qml
onClicked: root.viewModel.remove(index)   // good: intent goes to C++
```

Logic written in QML escapes the compiler's type checks, cannot be tested from C++, and
mixes with layout code. When a handler grows beyond a few lines, the code belongs in a C++
view model.
